Short facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that the petitioner as pre-emptor filed a case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Badalgachi being Misc. Case No. 140 of 1984, alleging inter alia that he is by purchase a co-sharer to the case jote while the preemptors are strangers thereto. It was also alleged that no notice under section 89 of the SAT Act was served upon him although he is a co-sharer to the case jote. Soon after coming to learned about the disputed transfer the pre-emptor filed the case on making statutory deposit, impleading necessary parties. 

 6. Mr. Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that in view of the proviso to section 96(3)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 that the transferee shall in no case is entitled to get compensation money in excess of the amount of money stated in the deed of transfer, the learned courts below evidently erred in law in holding the consideration money to be Tk. 8,000.00 in place of Tk. 3.000.00 as mentioned in the kabala under pre-emption and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate further 

 9. Now coming to the question as to whether the transferee can claim compensation money in excess of the amount stated in deed of transfer, we may profitably refer to the provision of section 96(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The proviso to section 96(3) of the S.A.T. Act specifically mention that the transferee shall in no case, to be entitled to claim compensation money in excess of the amount of money stated in deed of transfer. In the face of this clear provision of law there is absolutely no scope for speculation or any investigation as to what money was actually paid an consideration of the disputed transfer. Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 makes its abundantly clear that for the purpose of an application for pre-emption, the value of the subject matter of .pre-emption must be taken to be the amount of the consideration money mentioned in the deed of transfer. It is thus not open to any party to plead or prove that the actual price paid for the subject-matter of pre-emption was more than not what was actually stated in the deed of transfer. In the face of the clear language of the statute, the value of the subject-matter of pre-emption must be taken to be the amount of consideration money stated in the deed of transfer under challenge. We get instance support to this our view in the case of Ajit and others Vs. Hacharaddin Pradhan, reported in 18 DLR at page 632. A similar view has been taken in the case of Abdul Hossain Howlader and others Vs. Pulin Behar: Sikdar, reported in 22 DLR at page 535. The facts and circumstances of the present case fully apply to the facts and circumstances of the cited decisions referred to above and as such there is not scope to investigate or speculate as to what money was actually paid to the vendor by the vendee in the face of this clear statutory provision and consistent judicial pronouncements. In the facts of the case, I am constrained to hold that the learned Courts below evidently erred in law in fixing the consideration money at Tk. 8000.00, although in the kabala under pre-eruption the consideration money was specifically stated to be Tk. 3000.00. In the face of the specific statutory bar the pre-emptor is not at all entitled to claim any money above the amount specifically mentioned in the disputed deed of transfer. The pre-emptors are thus entitled to get only Tk. 3000.00 along with the statutory compensation thereon and not Tk. 8000.00 as the consideration money as wrongly found by the learned Courts below. For the reasons stated above, it must be held that the learned Courts below evidently erred in law in passing the impugned judgment on erroneous view of law and the same has occasioned failure of justice.
